papers.title_in_file: Gate teleportation-assisted routing for quantum algorithms
papers.version_note: arXiv:2502.04138v2, 14 Apr 2025; text matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A compilation study proposing Routing with Teleported Gates (RTG), which adds gate-teleportation virtual edges through unused qubits to SWAP-based routing, benchmarked on depth and CNOT counts for an IBM Eagle r3 topology segment.

existing.note: The paper also gives the assumed values (gate time three times, error probability ten times the native two-qubit values) in the same paragraph; see the new assertions.
existing.value: The authors state that their analysis uses values for teleported gates that they expect to be achievable in future devices, and note that current devices exhibit significantly higher error probabilities.
quotes: we chose to use values that we expect to be achievable in future devices
current devices exhibit significantly higher error probabilities
existing.certainty_reason: Section 3.1, p.9: the paper's statement of its own setup.

existing.note: The conclusion range (10 to 20%) differs from the abstract range (10 to 25%); the Section 3.1 results exclude the teleportation circuits themselves (Section 3.2, p.11). Both noted in new assertions.
existing.value: The authors state in the conclusions that teleportation-assisted routing can reduce circuit depth by 10 to 20% compared to a native line topology, and that the overhead introduced by auxiliary qubits must be carefully managed.
quotes: teleportation-assisted routing can reduce circuit depth by 10 to 20% compared to a native line topology
The overhead introduced by auxiliary qubits during teleportation must be carefully managed
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

existing.note: As stored (no number). The abstract's range is 10 to 25%; the paper's own Section 3.2 says the Section 3.1 reductions are an upper bound reached with virtual edges alone.
existing.value: The authors report a depth reduction in the routing of selected algorithms compared to regular routing without using teleported gates.
quotes: depth reduction in the routing of selected algorithms compared to regular routing without using teleported gates
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that they developed the Routing with Teleported Gates (RTG) method, a systematic approach designed to identify optimal virtual connections and routing pathways utilizing these connections.
quotes: we have developed the Routing with Teleported Gates (RTG) method, a systematic approach designed to identify optimal virtual connections and routing pathways utilizing these connections
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1, p.4: the paper defines its own method.

assertions.value: The authors state that they introduce gate teleportation as an add-on to existing SWAP-based routing and mapping methods, selectively teleporting specific gates.
quotes: We introduce gate teleportation as an add-on to existing SWAP-based routing and mapping methods.
This hybrid approach selectively employs teleportation for specific gates
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1, p.4: the paper's statement of its own scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that teleporting a CNOT gate through an auxiliary path with N qubits requires N + 1 CNOT gate operations and N mid-circuit measurements, of which only two CNOT gates operate directly on the data qubits.
quotes: Teleporting a CNOT gate through an auxiliary path with N qubits requires N + 1 CNOT gate operations and N mid-circuit measurements.
only two of these CNOT gates operate directly on the data qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own counting statement for a protocol they take from Ref. 33; no derivation in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper credits Ref. [33] for the CNOT teleportation method; the counts are stated, not derived here.

assertions.value: The authors state that controlled U teleportation requires N CNOT gate operations, one controlled U gate, and N mid-circuit measurements, and that the depth of these teleportation circuits remains constant regardless of the distance N.
quotes: controlled U teleportation requires N CNOT gate operations, one controlled U gate, and N mid-circuit measurements
the depth of these teleportation circuits remains constant regardless of the distance N
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a derivation in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that teleporting controlled gates requires both the target and control qubits to be locally connected with pre-entangled auxiliary qubits in a 1D chain topology, or at least connected to their nearest neighbours.
quotes: The teleportation of controlled gates requires both the target and control qubits to be locally connected with pre-entangled auxiliary qubits in a 1D chain topology or at least connected to their nearest neighbours.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2, p.4: the paper's statement of the conditions of its protocol.

assertions.value: The authors state that virtual edges differ from native physical connections in two key aspects: the gate times are longer, and the gate errors are higher than those of native two qubit gates.
quotes: virtual edges differ from native physical connections in two key aspects: the gate times are longer, and the gate errors are higher than those of native two qubit gates
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2, p.5: the paper's model of its own virtual edges.

assertions.value: The authors define the temporal depth as the maximum cumulative gate execution time along any path from the start to the end of the circuit, estimated from the directed acyclic graph representation of the circuit.
quotes: The temporal depth is defined as the maximum cumulative gate execution time along any path from the start to the end of the circuit.
The temporal depth is estimated from the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) [10] representation of the circuit
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2, p.6: the paper's own definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that the RTG search is a heuristic algorithm that primarily employs a greedy heuristic combined with randomized transpilation with the SABRE routing method.
quotes: we develop and benchmark a heuristic search algorithm, which takes into account the connectivity requirements of the circuit.
The algorithm primarily employs a greedy heuristic combined with randomized transpilation with the SABRE routing method.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2, p.7: the paper describes its own algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state that the search can be constrained to connections that are not used repeatedly, for example a limit such that only connections repeated twice or less in the whole algorithm are considered, because repeated teleported gates may not yield better performance.
quotes: multiple implementations of the teleported gate may not always yield better performance, given the increased error rates and the cost of reset operations required on the auxiliary qubits after every teleported gate operation through the same path
a limit can be set such that only connections repeated twice or less in the whole algorithm are considered
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2, p.7: the paper's own search constraint.

assertions.value: The authors state that the noise-aware RTG method estimates an error cost for all the two-qubit gates of the algorithm with a formula taken from Ref. [40], and that different weights can be assigned to the depth and error-cost criteria.
quotes: In the noise-aware RTG method, the error cost C2q for all the two-qubit gates of the algorithm is estimated with the formula [40]:
it is also possible to assign different weights to these criteria, allowing for a more flexible optimization
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2, pp.7-8: the paper defines its own noise-aware variant.

assertions.value: The authors state that they employ 15-qubit benchmark circuits from the Munich Quantum Toolkit Benchmark Library (MQT Bench) [41], with an initial qubit layout that is a simple line topology [qubits no. 18–32 in Fig. 4(a)] on a segment of the IBM 127-qubit Eagle r3 topology.
quotes: we employ 15-qubit benchmark circuits from the Munich Quantum Toolkit Benchmark Library (MQT Bench) [41]
The initial qubit layout is chosen as a simple line topology [qubits no. 18–32 in Fig. 4(a)]
we assess their performance on a segment of the IBM 127-qubit Eagle r3 processor topology
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.1, pp.8-9: the paper's own benchmark setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the benchmark analysis they consider CNOT gate teleportation and assume the gate time for teleported CNOT gates is three times the native two-qubit gate time and the average error probability of teleported gates is ten times that of native two-qubit gates.
quotes: we consider the CNOT gate teleportation and assume the gate time for teleported CNOT gates is tgtele = 3t2gq and average error probability Pgtele = 10Pg2q
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.1, p.9: the paper's own assumed parameters.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer printed the symbols flat (tgtele, t2gq, Pgtele, Pg2q); the reading as ratios of teleported to native values follows the sentence.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as reported in Ref. [33], the teleported-gate error probability is approximately 100 times the native two-qubit value for teleportation over a distance of 10 qubits, and that these values come from the first generation of processors capable of mid-circuit measurements and feed-forward.
quotes: as reported in Ref. [33], Pgtele ≈ 100Pg2q, for a distance of teleportation over 10 qubits
As these values are obtained from the first generation of processors capable for mid-circuit measurements and feed-forward
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 33.
assertions.reader_inference: With the assumed ratio of ten in the same paragraph, the cited ratio of about 100 shows the analysis assumes errors about ten times lower than the cited experiment.

assertions.value: The authors report that the benchmark results show a reduction in circuit depth across all benchmark cases except for QAOA, and that the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm achieves approximately 18% reduction in depth with both RTG and noise-aware RTG.
quotes: The results demonstrate a reduction in circuit depth across all cases except for QAOA.
The Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm achieves
approximately 18% reduction in depth when utilizing both RTG and noise-aware RTG methods
assertions.reader_inference: The benchmark set is 15-qubit circuits on one line layout, with the assumed parameters above. The bar values other than 18% are in the figure image only.

assertions.value: The authors report that performance decreases for the graph state preparation and QFT benchmarks when noise-aware routing is considered.
quotes: However, performance decreases for the graph state preparation and QFT benchmarks when noise-aware routing is considered (noise-aware RTG).

assertions.value: The authors report that QAOA shows no depth reduction with CNOT gate teleportation; they explain that RZZ interactions decompose into two CNOT gates separated by a single qubit Z rotation, so each connection involves more than two CNOT gates and the search avoids repeated use of the same connection, and they suggest teleporting RZZ gates may be more effective.
quotes: which are then decomposed into two CNOT gates separated by a single qubit Z rotation
each connection involves more than two CNOT gates, and the heuristic search is constrained to avoid repeated use of the same connections
This suggests that teleporting RZZ gates may be a more effective option than teleporting CNOT gates directly in this case.
assertions.certainty_reason: An explanation offered by the authors; the CNOT-teleport QAOA bar is in Figure 5 only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the effectiveness of the RTG method is highly dependent on the structure of an algorithm and the specific gate operations involved.
quotes: These findings highlight that the effectiveness of the RTG method is highly dependent on the structure of an algorithm and the specific gate operations involved.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' reading of results from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Section 3.1 results use virtual edges without the actual teleportation circuits, and that the observed depth reduction therefore represents the maximum possible improvement expected with virtual edges alone.
quotes: In Sec. 3.1, we have demonstrated depth reduction by incorporating optimal virtual edges into the coupling map.
However, we have not yet included the actual teleportation
Therefore, the observed depth reduction represents the maximum possible improvement one can expect with virtual edges alone.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections 3.1-3.2: the paper's own statement of the scope of its Section 3.1 numbers.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's 10 to 25% and the conclusion's 10 to 20% rest partly on these virtual-edge figures; Table 1 gives lower figures for the implemented circuits.

assertions.value: The authors define the virtual coupling map case as one where possible additional connections are added to the initial coupling map without considering the actual implementation of virtual connections, an ideal case giving the maximum reduction in circuit depth for a specific set of virtual connections.
quotes: represents the case where possible additional connections are added to the initial coupling map without considering the actual implementation of virtual connections.
This situation represents an ideal case, demonstrating the maximum reduction in circuit depth that can be achieved with a specific set of virtual connections.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2, p.11: the paper's own definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the Deutsch-Jozsa case study the baseline circuit is transpiled with 9–15 qubits arranged in a line topology, the RTG virtual edges use CNOT gate teleportation, and SABRE is the base routing method in all transpilations.
quotes: As a baseline, the circuit is first transpiled with 9–15 qubits arranged in a line topology.
we incorporate the optimal virtual edges identified by the RTG method for CNOT gate teleportation into the circuit
Note that in all of the transpilations, we use the SABRE as the base method for routing.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2, p.11: the paper's own setup.

assertions.value: The authors report for the Deutsch-Jozsa case study that the implemented teleportation circuits reduce circuit depth compared to the line coupling map, but by less than the ideal coupling map with virtual connections predicts.
quotes: The results demonstrate a reduction in circuit depth compared to the corresponding line coupling map; however, this reduction is less than anticipated with an ideal coupling map incorporating virtual connections (Virtual c. map).
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 text layer, qubits 9 to 15: line depth 35, 42, 51, 53, 59, 62, 67; implemented depth 31, 38, 43, 43, 52, 52, 62; table reduction (Impl.) 11, 10, 16, 19, 12, 16, 7 percent against Expected 11, 12, 25, 34, 22, 29, 15 percent. Single-run compilation counts; no variance reported.

assertions.value: The authors report for the Deutsch-Jozsa case study that, in the physical implementation, the total number of CNOT gates is considerably higher than in the line topology, while the number of CNOT gates directly acting on data qubits remains relatively similar.
quotes: In the case of physical implementation, the total number of CNOT gates
is considerably higher than in the line topology.
Nonetheless, the number of CNOT gates directly acting on data qubits remains relatively similar.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1: CNOT counts on line map 20 to 30; implemented 28 to 61 total, 18 to 33 on data qubits.

assertions.value: The authors state that a shallower circuit helps to reduce decoherence, resulting in improved overall fidelity, and that the depth reduction is therefore highly relevant for near-term quantum devices.
quotes: A shallower circuit helps to reduce decoherence, resulting in improved overall fidelity.
the reduction in circuit depth discussed here is highly relevant for near-term quantum devices
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a fidelity measurement in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: No fidelity, noise simulation or hardware run is reported; the claim is about depth only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QAOA case study uses a QAOA Ansatz circuit for the Max-Cut problem with 9 to 15 qubits, an initial line coupling map of qubits 18–32, and two fixed virtual connections between qubits 20-28 and 22-30, physically routed through auxiliary qubit paths.
quotes: we consider a QAOA Ansatz circuit for the Max-Cut problem using 9 to 15 qubits
The initial mapping is a line coupling map of qubits 18–32.
adding two virtual connections between qubits 20-28 and 22-30
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.3, p.12: the paper's own setup.

assertions.value: The authors report for the QAOA case study that controlled-U teleportation again demonstrates depth reduction, with an extent that is highly dependent on the number of qubits, which they attribute to using two fixed connections that were not optimized for each qubit number.
quotes: The results again demonstrate depth reduction with teleported gates; however, the extent of the reduction is highly dependent on the number of qubits.
because the connections were not optimized for the specific number of qubits; instead, two fixed connections were used in all instances.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 2 text layer, qubits 9 to 15: Impl. depth reduction 11, 4, 25, 19, 9, 13, 24 percent against Expected 17, 23, 40, 29, 31, 25, 33 percent.

assertions.value: The authors report for the QAOA case study that the total number of CNOT gates is relatively high but the number of CNOTs acting on the data qubits is comparable to that of the line map, and that the number of teleported gates is relatively high because no constraints were introduced.
quotes: The total number of CNOT gates in the circuit is relatively high, but the number of CNOTs acting on the data qubits is comparable to that of the line map.
the number of teleported gates is relatively high in this scenario, as no constraints were introduced

assertions.value: The authors state that, while the results show potential, they may not translate into optimal performance on current quantum devices due to these limitations.
quotes: Consequently, while the results show potential, they may not translate into optimal performance on current quantum devices due to these limitations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.3, p.13: the paper's own stated limit.

assertions.value: The authors state in the conclusions that teleporting CNOT gates was generally effective, and that their QAOA case study showed teleporting RZZ gates using controlled-U teleportation provided better performance.
quotes: While teleporting CNOT gates was generally effective, our case study on QAOA circuits showed that teleporting RZZ gates using controlled-U teleportation provided better performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the scaling of auxiliary qubit usage depends on algorithmic requirements and the number of available qubits on the hardware, making it an adaptable strategy rather than a fixed overhead.
quotes: The scaling of auxiliary qubit usage depends on algorithmic requirements and the number of available qubits on the hardware, making it an adaptable strategy rather than a fixed overhead.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without a scaling measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the choice of the initial layout could also affect the results, and that the line layout used is a trivial choice for which alternative mapping strategies can be used equally.
quotes: While this particular layout is a trivial choice, alternative mapping strategies can be used equally with the RTG method.
Note that the choice of the initial layout could also affect the results
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections 3.1 and 4: the paper's own stated limit.

assertions.value: The authors state that future research could extend the method to more complex topologies and experimentally validate the proposed schemes.
quotes: Future research could extend this method to work with more complex topologies and experimentally validate the proposed schemes.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4, p.14: the paper's own stated open problem.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no hardware run of the full routing method; all results are compiled circuit depth and gate counts.

assertions.value: The authors state that the routing problem is closely related to the token-swapping problem, which is classified as NP-hard, so the routing problem is believed to belong to the same complexity class.
quotes: the routing problem is closely related to the token-swapping problem [6]
As the token-swapping problem is classified as NP-hard, the routing problem is believed to belong to the same complexity class [6, 7].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Refs. 6 and 7.

assertions.value: The authors state that two cited works show that mid-circuit measurements and feed-forward operations can be used to reduce the depth of circuits, which may decrease the effects of decoherence and increase the fidelity of quantum algorithms.
quotes: Both articles show that mid-circuit measurements and feed-forward operations can be used to reduce the depth of circuits, which may decrease the effects of decoherence and increase the fidelity of quantum algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Refs. 33 and 34.

assertions.value: The authors state that an analysis of the speed-up of the local operations and classical communication (LOCC) assisted routing technique over SWAP-based methods is studied in Ref. [35], as long as O(n) auxiliary qubits are allowed.
quotes: An in-depth analysis of the speed-up of the local operations and classical communication (LOCC) assisted routing technique over SWAP-based methods is studied in Ref. [35], as long as O(n) auxiliary qubits are allowed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 35.

assertions.value: The authors state that Ref. [36] proposes quantum teleportation as a complementary method in routing, where teleportation channels through ancillary qubits add virtual edges to the coupling map.
quotes: In Ref. [36], quantum teleportation is proposed as a complementary method in routing, where the possible teleportation channels through ancillary qubits add virtual edges to the coupling map
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 36.
assertions.reader_inference: Prior work already used virtual edges from teleportation channels; this paper's stated additions are gate teleportation and the noise-aware selection.
